children: This week’s market stories connected luxury cars, electric vehicles, robotaxis and ride-hailing into one crowded transportation narrative. Demand remains strong in some corners, while production changes and operational challenges reshape others.
Ferrari
reported stronger-than-expected results,
Uber
highlighted pressure from fuel costs and driver shortages and
Tesla
made room for its next autonomous-driving push.
Meanwhile,
Lyft
said robotaxis were not hurting its business, while Tesla’s European registrations surged as fuel prices climbed amid geopolitical tensions.
Ferrari’s Luce Is Sold Out Before Test Drives

Ferrari N.V. posted better-than-expected third-quarter results and increased its 2026 outlook. The company’s performance benefited from stronger interest in personalized vehicles, a more profitable product mix and currency headwinds that were less severe than anticipated. Its new Luce model is already sold out for 2027, even before customers begin test drives.
Uber Faces a Tougher International Road

Uber Technologies Inc. reported mixed third-quarter 2026 results. Uber generated $14.77 billion in quarterly revenue, a 10% increase from the same period last year. The figure also exceeded Wall Street’s $14.70 billion estimate, although the company’s international expansion is confronting driver shortages and rising fuel costs. The combination puts new emphasis on operating conditions outside Uber’s strongest markets, where supply challenges and higher expenses can complicate continued growth.
Tesla Is Preparing a Cybertruck Production Shift
Tesla Inc. CEO
Elon Musk

said production of the Cybertruck at the company’s Gigafactory Texas facility will wind down around mid-2027. The move is intended to create capacity for increased Cybercab production. Musk confirmed the plan in a late-Thursday post on X, writing, "Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production." The announcement puts the Cybertruck at the center of Tesla’s planned manufacturing shift, while Cybertruck production in Texas is scheduled to taper later in the decade.
Lyft Says Robotaxis Are Not Undermining Its Business

Lyft Inc. CEO David Risher said during the company’s third-quarter 2026 earnings call that autonomous driving and robotaxis were not negatively affecting Lyft’s ride-hailing operations. Asked whether robotaxis had influenced Lyft’s business in cities such as Austin, Risher declined to discuss any specific market in detail. He nevertheless said Lyft was "actually growing" in markets where autonomous vehicles operate. Risher’s comments came alongside details about Lyft’s activity in autonomous-vehicle markets and its partnership with Waymo.
Tesla Registrations Accelerate Across Europe

Tesla Inc. recorded sharp registration increases across several European markets as the automaker seeks to benefit from energy shocks linked to continuing geopolitical tensions. Registrations climbed 248% in Sweden and 131% in Norway. Spain recorded a 271% increase, while Denmark posted a 34% gain as fuel prices rose following the Iran war. The gains arrived as Tesla competed with
BYD
and other Chinese electric-vehicle manufacturers, which were also gaining ground across Europe.

title: Ferrari’s Sold-Out Luce, Tesla’s Cybertruck Pivot, Uber’s Roadblocks and More: This Week in Mobility
